name: Marco Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and have spent years answering event ticket calls and chats at a contact centre, at about the team's usual pace. I finished secondary school, use AI search every day, and work late shifts that pay above the usual rate; I still check the live seat map because an old layout can strand a family. I like solving a seat problem before a show starts, and I hate when a buyer reaches the door with a code that our desk marked fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ticket team the search shortcut is good for finding a seat change, provided we still check the event date. A fast answer for the wrong concert date is worse than a slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day and enjoy seeing where it saves clicks. My late shifts pay above the usual rate, and nine months of expenses are saved, so a small tool change would not shake our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the evening ticket calls and check each suggested seat against the live event map. In the first year of this plateau, I'd add some of the late-shift premium to savings and keep helping at my children's weekend sports matches, where I see how a crowd moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. A little less typing would let me listen longer when someone has bought the wrong date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the map catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A caller wanted three seats together, but the draft showed three in different rows. I moved the order before the family arrived at the venue and found out at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep adding to savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ines and I have a mortgage and two children, and the late premium is not guaranteed forever. Saving while it comes in leaves us choices if the rota changes.

S0.quote: A fast answer for the wrong concert date is worse than a slow one.
say: I would use the **search shortcut** while checking the event date and seat map.
I would avoid a **fast wrong answer** for a ticket buyer.
think: I use AI daily and enjoy a tool that **saves clicks**.
I have **nine months** saved and higher late-shift pay, so this small change feels safe.
do: Keep **evening ticket calls** and check seat suggestions against the live map.
Add part of the **late premium** to savings during the first year.
feel: **Comfortable**, with more time to listen to buyers.
fieldNote: Marco caught a **three-seat mismatch** before a family reached the venue.
His **nine-month reserve** and late premium make a mild change feel secure despite the mortgage and two children.

steps.text: Keep evening ticket calls and check suggested seats against the live event map
Add part of each late-shift premium payment to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the centre should test ticket changes on a busy sale night before claiming the new system can handle them. I'd offer to log the failures with the door staff, because they meet the customer when a code will not scan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take bookings and many changes that fill my shift. I might be useful testing the system, but one testing post could replace several late agents, and a lower-paid daytime role would change our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new ticket checker on twenty past seat changes and compare the results with the door team's records. In the first year after rollout, if my late hours fall and a posted paid venue-support role opens, I'd apply only if written wages and hours cover our bills; I'd keep this shift until I sign another offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious and uneasy. I like testing the machine, but I don't want to learn the result from a smaller pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the door team tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They can tell me which codes failed at the entrance and which customers had to stand aside. A smooth ticket chat means little if a family is still stuck outside the venue door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the venue role pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the full week's pay, not just the hourly rate, and stay where I am if it cannot cover the mortgage. Nine months saved is not a reason to accept a lasting pay cut.

S1.quote: A smooth ticket chat means little if a family is still stuck outside the venue door.
say: I would test **busy ticket changes** before accepting claims of better service.
I would compare failures with **door staff** who see stranded buyers.
think: I could lose **booking work** from the late shift.
I might get a **testing role**, but one post could replace several agents and lower pay would hurt.
do: Learn the **ticket checker** on twenty old seat changes with door records.
Apply for a **posted paid venue role** if late hours fall and written wages and hours cover bills.
Keep my **current shift** until a new offer is signed.
feel: **Curious and uneasy** about the tool and the pay packet.
fieldNote: Marco uses **door scans** as a check on tidy chat replies.
He compares **weekly income** before leaving the late premium, despite nine months saved for mortgage and school costs.

steps.text: Learn the ticket checker on twenty past seat changes and compare door records
Apply for posted paid venue work after late-hour cuts only with written bill-covering wages and hours
Keep the late call shift until another offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could sell tickets, change seats, and settle complaints without our headsets. I'd ask for cut dates in writing and a route for customers whose tickets fail at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side of my job could go by 2028, even if I have years of experience. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, so the venue floor has a few years, but I cannot call it safe for life. Our nine-month reserve would give us time to test a real offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager for a written staffing date now and stop adding to our planned room renovation. In the first year after AGI arrives, if the call role ends, I'd take an advertised paid event-steward shift only if its hours and wages cover our mortgage; I'd ask about crowd-safety training before paying for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can do more than wait. I want to see the pay sheet for a whole event month before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stewarding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help direct parents at my children's sports matches, and I like solving a problem where people are standing. A paid event night is harder, and robots around 2031 may change crowd work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use savings to start an events business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not before I know the wages and the demand. I'd use the reserve for the mortgage during a search, not for a website and a box of printed badges.

S2.quote: I want to see the pay sheet for a whole event month before changing jobs.
say: I would ask for **written cut dates** before 2028.
I would keep a **human ticket appeal** route at venue doors.
think: I expect AGI could take **ticket calls** by 2028.
I see **2031 robots** as a later risk for event floors, while nine months saved allows a careful search.
do: Ask for a **staffing date** now and stop funding the room renovation.
Take an **advertised paid steward shift** after a cut only if monthly hours and wages cover the mortgage.
Check **crowd-safety training** before paying any fee.
feel: **Anxious**, yet able to inspect a real month of wages.
fieldNote: Marco has **sports-match experience** with crowds, but recognises paid steward work is harder.
He wants **monthly event wages**, not an attractive one-night rate that could leave quiet weeks unpaid.

steps.text: Pause spending on the planned room renovation
Take advertised paid steward work after call cuts only if monthly wages and hours cover mortgage
Request written staffing dates now to time applications for paid venue work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to test event-floor work and get proper training attached to a real vacancy. I'd ask the centre to publish late-shift numbers yearly while people can still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could take paid steward shifts before 2031 and see whether the income is steady enough for the house. AGI still reaches tickets then; robots follow around 2034, so I would not sign a long venue contract on the strength of one good night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my ticket calls and ask a venue for a paid trial on a busy event night this year. If it posts a paid steward place and covers crowd-safety classes on paid time, I'd take the required course; in the first year after AGI arrives, if my late calls end, I'd switch only for a written offer whose monthly wages and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful, not rushed. Five years lets me find out whether the job pays when there is no sold-out show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a trial night show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the start time, the quiet hours between events, and whether the team is paid for setup. A packed room looks busy, but a mortgage needs pay on ordinary weeks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for safety classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The venue should pay the fee and the class hours if the certificate is needed for its posted role. I would not spend our reserve on a badge without a job behind it.

S3.quote: A packed room looks busy, but a mortgage needs pay on ordinary weeks too.
say: I would ask for **real steward vacancies** with paid training.
I would request **yearly late-shift numbers** from the centre.
think: I could test **paid event shifts** before 2031 while keeping ticket wages.
I would avoid a **long venue contract** because 2034 robots may change floor work.
do: Keep **ticket calls** and request a paid busy-night trial.
Take **required crowd-safety classes** only for a posted paid job with venue-funded fees and paid hours.
Switch after 2031 only for a **written offer** with monthly wages and hours covering bills.
feel: **Watchful**, with time to test ordinary-week pay.
fieldNote: Marco asks about paid setup and **quiet weeks**, not just sold-out nights.
He keeps **course fees** behind a posted paid vacancy and venue-paid class time.

steps.text: Keep ticket calls while requesting a paid busy-night venue trial
Try a paid steward shift if a venue posts a place
Take required crowd-safety classes only for posted paid work with venue-funded fees and paid time
Switch after call cuts only for written monthly wages and hours covering household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives workers time to measure jobs properly, not take the first course a manager recommends. I'd ask for annual paid agent hours so the team can see when the late rota shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 the mortgage may still be there, although our children will be older. AGI reaches ticket calls in 2036 and robots reach hands-on work around 2039, so event floors need checking too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the evening calls and add to our reserve while the premium lasts. Over the decade I'd take paid event trials when posted and compare full-month wages; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd move only if call hours fall and a signed venue offer covers our bills and family schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with a little caution. Ten years before AGI reaches my ticket calls in 2036 lets me compare a full pay month, not just a bright event night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a signed venue offer with dependable monthly hours and enough pay, yes. I would not leave the late premium because a manager said the future looked exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I might work some evenings at a venue and still be home for their matches when I can. They should not have to guess why I missed a Saturday.

S4.quote: Ten years before AGI reaches my ticket calls in 2036 lets me compare a full pay month, not just a bright event night.
say: I would ask for **annual paid agent hours** as the late rota changes.
I would compare **full-month wages** before switching jobs.
think: I may still owe on the **mortgage** at 53.
I know **2039 robots** may change venue floors after AGI takes ticket calls.
do: Keep **evening calls** and add to savings while the premium lasts.
Take **posted paid event trials** and compare full-month wages.
Move after 2036 only if **call hours fall**, with signed bill-covering venue pay, dependable monthly hours and a workable family schedule.
feel: **Steady**, with time to check real pay.
fieldNote: Marco tests **monthly income** rather than judging the busy feel of one event night.
He wants his children to know **why evening work** sometimes takes him from their matches.

steps.text: Keep evening ticket calls while the higher rate continues
Add part of late-shift pay to family savings
Take posted paid event trials and compare monthly wages
Move after 2036 if calls fall with signed bill-covering venue wages and dependable family-compatible monthly hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the ticket calls could go before I know what a month of paid venue work earns. Written cut dates, posted steward shifts with mortgage-covering monthly pay, and venue-funded safety classes on paid time would help. Nine months saved gives us time to compare offers, not a reason to buy a business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who helps a buyer at the door when a ticket code fails after a perfect chat answer. A venue worker needs the authority to fix a failed ticket at the door, not just hand out another printed apology.

headlineQuote: A venue worker needs the authority to fix a failed ticket at the door, not just hand out another printed apology.
portrait: Marco is a **43-year-old experienced agent** on ticket calls, with average skill and secondary schooling.
He earns **higher late-shift pay**, has about nine months saved, a partner, two school-age children, a mortgage, and many nearby centres.
He uses AI **daily** and compares desk answers with venue door records before trusting speed figures.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens ticket calls; slower timelines let him test paid steward work against full-month household bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end ticket wages before he knows whether venue work pays enough every month.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut dates**, posted paid steward shifts, and venue-funded safety training would help him judge a switch.
